did_you_know.text: Did you know? Sennacherib king of Assyria came to Judah after the events described earlier in the chapter and camped against its fortified cities in order to conquer them.
Did you know? Hezekiah consulted with his officials and warriors and stopped up the springs outside Jerusalem so that the Assyrians would not find readily available water sources.
Did you know? Hezekiah repaired the broken sections of the wall, added towers and another wall, fortified the City of David, and prepared many weapons and shields.
Did you know? In his speech to the people, Hezekiah contrasted the human strength of the king of Assyria—“an arm of flesh”—with the help of the Lord, who was with Judah.
Did you know? While Sennacherib himself was at Lachish, he sent his servants to Jerusalem to intimidate Hezekiah and its inhabitants and force them to surrender.
Did you know? The Assyrian messengers shouted in Hebrew to the people of Jerusalem who were on the wall, intending to frighten and terrify them so that they could capture the city.
Did you know? Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz prayed and cried out to the Lord, after which Jerusalem’s deliverance from the Assyrian army is described.

Did you know? According to the text, the Lord sent an angel who struck down the mighty warriors, officials, and commanders in the camp of the king of Assyria; Sennacherib returned to his land in disgrace.
Did you know? Hezekiah became mortally ill, prayed to the Lord, and the Lord answered him and gave him a sign.

Did you know? The visit of the Babylonian officials to Hezekiah, who came to inquire about the sign that had occurred in the land, is described as a test in which God left him in order to know what was in his heart.
Did you know? Hezekiah was buried with great honor in the upper section of the tombs of the descendants of David, and after his death his son Manasseh succeeded him as king.
